claim.primary_outcome_paraphrase: A CNN replaces the least-squares step of classical de-homogenization. The resulting single-scale designs come within 7-25% of the homogenization-based reference performance, at a small fraction of the cost. The body quantifies the saving as about 5-10x over least-squares de-homogenization.
claim.key_phrase: within 7−25% of the homogenization-based solution at a fraction of the computational cost
claim.location: Abstract (first quantitative comparison with a classical method; §5.1 rule 1). The cost part is qualitative in the abstract and is quantified in Sec. 4.2.1 (p. 18) and the Conclusions (p. 22) as a factor of 5 to 10 over state-of-the-art de-homogenization
claim.claimed_speedup_basis: Stated as a factor of 5 to 10 (Sec. 4.2.1, p. 18; Conclusions, p. 22); the lower bound is entered. It is a cross-paper estimate. Groen et al. [16] report about 10 s for 80x40 -> 1600x800 on another laptop. This work needs about 1.3 s for 60x30 -> 1440x720 and about 2.2 s for 60x30 -> 2400x1200 on a single Intel Core i7 2.6 GHz CPU. Ratios: 10/1.3 = 7.7 and 10/2.2 = 4.5 [derived]. Training (about 1 h on a Titan X GPU) and the homogenization-based optimization that supplies the input are not counted.
claim.alternatives: (1) Sec. 4.2.1, p. 18: vs standard TO with top88, 16 s and 87 s per iteration at 1440x720 and 2400x1200, times an assumed 1000 continuation iterations = 16,000 s and 87,000 s. The paper calls the method four orders of magnitude faster (16,000/1.3 = 12,300 and 87,000/2.2 = 39,500 [derived]). No top88 design is produced. (2) Fig. 1 caption, p. 1: 200x50 -> 8000x2000 in 15 s on a laptop, compliance within 17% of the homogenization solution. (3) Introduction, p. 3: about 2 s for 2400x1200; no comparator number. (4) Tables 2-5 and App. A Table 1, quality only: Cf*Vf / (Cref*Vref) = 1.0677-1.5260 over all 30 cases [derived]; mean 1.257 and 1.223 (60x30 input, Table 2), 1.130 (240x120, Table 3), 1.224 (double-clamped, Table 4), 1.119 (L-shaped, Table 5) [derived; the text gives 25.7%, 22.3%, 13%, 22.4% and about 12%].

baseline.classical_method: Primary: least-squares de-homogenization of homogenization-based TO results (Groen and Sigmund 2018 [16]); its time is cited, not run (Sec. 4.2.1). Quality reference for every case: the rank-2 homogenization-based TO solution that supplies the CNN input (Sec. 2.1, eq. 1; code by J. P. Groen per the Acknowledgements). Alternative speed comparator: SIMP with the top88 MATLAB code at the fine resolution, per-iteration time measured, iteration count assumed (Sec. 4.2.1)
baseline.implementation: Least-squares de-homogenization: not described (cited result from [16]). top88: the public 88-line MATLAB code (footnote 1, p. 18). Homogenization TO: in-house code (Acknowledgements). Proposed: fully convolutional network with post-processing (skeletonize, distance transform) (Sec. 2.2-2.3, App. B)
baseline.solver: not stated for any classical method (top88 as published uses a sparse direct solve [recalled, not verified in-session]); the authors note that direct solvers break down at 16.5 million elements and multigrid would be needed (Sec. 4.2.1)
baseline.hardware_classical: [16]: a laptop of unstated model (Sec. 4.2.1). top88: not stated [same laptop inferred]
baseline.hardware_ml: Training on an NVIDIA Titan X GPU; all reported de-homogenization times on a single Intel Core i7 2.6 GHz CPU (Sec. 4.1)
baseline.problem_size: Coarse homogenization meshes 60x30, 120x60 and 240x120 (Michell cantilever), 200x50 (double-clamped), 80x80 [inferred from hc = 1/80] (L-shaped); fine meshes from 1440x720 (about 2.1 million DOFs [derived]) up to 5760x2880 (16.5 million elements) and 8000x2000 (Tables 2-5, Figs. 10-15). [16] comparator: 80x40 -> 1600x800
baseline.classical_iterations: [16]: not stated. top88: about 1000 iterations assumed for a continuation strategy, citing [35]; no run to convergence (Sec. 4.2.1). Homogenization TO: solved until convergence; criterion not stated (Sec. 4)
baseline.classical_time: [16]: about 10 s for 80x40 -> 1600x800 (cited, Sec. 4.2.1). top88: 16 s per iteration at 1440x720 and 87 s at 2400x1200; totals 16,000 s and 87,000 s extrapolated (Sec. 4.2.1). Homogenization TO time: not stated
baseline.ml_time: Tables 2-5 and App. A Table 1, per case on the CPU: 1.26-1.33 s (1440x720), 2.10-2.23 s (2400x1200), 5.38-5.85 s (2880x1440), 23.30-24.02 s (5760x2880), 7.12-15.80 s (double-clamped), 4.96-7.53 s (L-shaped). A forward pass takes a few milliseconds on a GPU (Sec. 4.1)
baseline.training_time: about 1 hour for the full two-step training (15 epochs) on an NVIDIA Titan X GPU (Sec. 4.1)
baseline.data_generation_cost: not stated; 20,000 synthetic orientation fields from sums of low-frequency sines (Sec. 3, Sec. 4.1); no TO runs are needed for training [cost small, inferred]
baseline.quality_metric: Compliance Cf and volume fraction Vf of the de-homogenized fine-mesh design against the homogenization reference (Cref, Vref); performance ratio Cf*Vf / (Cref*Vref), lower is better (Tables 2-5, App. A Table 1). How Cf is computed is not described [FE analysis on the fine mesh inferred]
baseline.quality_gap: All 30 cases: performance ratio 1.0677-1.5260, i.e. 6.8-52.6% worse than the homogenization reference [derived]; the abstract qualifies its 7-25% as holding for a suitable choice of parameters. Volume overshoot: the text gives 5.7% and 2.4% mean (Table 2) and 2.3% (Table 4); the printed values give 5.4%, 2.0%, 2.5%, and 9.3% for the L-shaped beam [derived]. The quality of the timed comparator ([16]) is not reported

R1.evidence: Abstract, Sec. 4.2.1 (pp. 17-18) and Conclusions (p. 22): the 5-10x factor compares this work's CPU times (about 1.3 s and 2.2 s) with a time cited from [16] (about 10 s, 80x40 -> 1600x800) on another laptop, which the authors call not directly comparable. Quality is reported only against the homogenization reference (performance ratio 1.0677-1.5260 over 30 cases [derived]; 7-25% in the abstract for suitable parameters), and the authors present that loss as a trade-off for cost (p. 19). The quality of [16]'s designs is not reported and no matching of quality or budget is attempted, so matching is loose (§5.3 R1 partial). Fail would apply if [16]'s designs were shown to be measurably better. The alternative top88 comparison (four orders of magnitude) produces no top88 design and would fail R1 (R1-no-quality) if taken as primary.

R2.evidence: Sec. 4.1 and 4.2.1: both sides are timed on laptops (CNN on a single Intel Core i7 2.6 GHz CPU; [16] on a laptop of unstated model and device), and the ML side runs on a CPU, so (c) does not apply. The abstract gives no baseline figure (b). No iteration count exists for [16], so (d) and (e) cannot be derived. The authors flag that the cross-paper times are not directly comparable. Unsure, so pass. Pointer for the top88 alternative: 16 s and 87 s per iteration at about 2.1 and 5.8 million DOFs [derived] can be checked for (e) with the project's baseline at the same size; the 1000 iterations are assumed, not run.

R3.evidence: Sec. 4.1: training time (about 1 h on a Titan X for 15 epochs) is reported. The cost of generating the 20,000 synthetic orientation fields is not stated (it needs no TO runs; small [inferred]). No break-even or amortization is given, and the claim is not explicitly limited to per-query use. For C3 [derived, cross-hardware, rough]: 3,600 s of training over a saving of about 8.7 s per use vs [16] gives about 400 uses; vs the top88 alternative, fewer than one use.

R4.evidence: Tables 2-5 and App. A Table 1: compliance and volume fraction are reported for the post-processed design in every case (all 30 cases, no selection); FE evaluation is inferred, as the method is not described. Volume overshoot is visible per case and discussed (Sec. 4.2-4.3). Non-load-carrying boundary artefacts appear in many designs (Sec. 4.2, p. 16) but are not counted, and no disconnection or failure count is given.

reporting.n_test_cases: 30 de-homogenization cases [derived]: Michell cantilever 12 (60x30 input, Table 2), 6 (120x60, App. A Table 1), 6 (240x120, Table 3); double-clamped beam 4 (Table 4); L-shaped beam 2 (Table 5); plus the Fig. 1 example

notes: Screening code I-SPEED confirmed. Primary outcome: the abstract pairs a quantitative quality gap (7-25% from the homogenization reference) with a qualitative cost claim tied to avoiding the least-squares problems of classical de-homogenization; stratum speed because the primary outcome compares cost. Its factor comes from Sec. 4.2.1 and the Conclusions (5-10x). Under §5.1 rule 4 the four-orders-of-magnitude claim vs top88 (Sec. 4.2.1 only) is an alternative; it rests on an assumed 1000 iterations and has no top88 design. Direction coded similar_or_mixed: faster but measurably worse than the reference. The abstract range is the favourable subset: all 30 cases span 6.8-52.6% [derived]; the Conclusions qualify the 7-25% as holding before post-processing, without explanation. Small inconsistencies: the text gives mean volume overshoots of 5.7% and 2.4% for Table 2, the printed values give 5.4% and 2.0% [derived]; App. A reuses the labels 'Table 1' and 'Figure 1'; the Adam betas are printed as β1 = 0.9, β1 = 0.99 (Sec. 4.1). OOD = yes because training uses only synthetic sine-based orientation fields, while every test input comes from homogenization-based TO with its own domain, loads and supports [inferred]. Code: github.com/elingaard/deep-dehom (GitHub API 2026-09-24: public, created 2021-10-17, no licence declared; README calls it experimental; pre-trained model notebook and Output_TO homogenization designs). It is not cited in arXiv v1. Data: DTU Data collection 5684665, linked to the version-of-record DOI; its 'pretrained models' item (doi 10.11583/DTU.16902961) is CC BY 4.0; the synthetic-data item's licence was not read. retest_candidate false: no code licence (PROTOCOL §10), and the timed comparator (least-squares de-homogenization [16]) is not provided. The CNN-side times could be re-run from the notebook if a human accepts the unlicensed code. Version: arXiv v1 coded; the open-access version of record (CMAME 388, 114197) could not be read by script and may differ, including any availability statements. Adjudicator check (2026-09-24): ScienceDirect again returned a captcha page (HTTP 403); the DTU Orbit record page lists the CC BY 'Final published version' (volume 388, article 114197, 22 pages), but its PDF link returned a Cloudflare challenge (HTTP 403). Neither was bypassed, so arXiv v1 remains the coded text. COI check: no author named Jun Wang.

R1.reason: Quality is reported, but only against the homogenization reference (Tables 2-5; abstract 7-25%). The timed comparator [16] is a cited time on other hardware whose design quality is never given (Sec. 4.2.1, p. 18). The text establishes neither fail condition: the CNN output is not shown worse than [16]'s output, and a quality comparison does exist. What remains is the §5.3 R1 partial case, quality reported with loose matching.

R2.reason: For the primary comparator [16], the text establishes none of (a)-(e): the abstract gives no baseline figure, both timings come from laptops (this work: a single Intel Core i7 CPU, Sec. 4.1), and [16]'s iterations and implementation are not given (Sec. 4.2.1, p. 18). The second coder's partial concerns top88, which is the alternative comparator, and unsure means pass.

claimed_speedup.reason: The article states only a range, a factor of 5 to 10 (Sec. 4.2.1, p. 18; Conclusions, p. 22), so the conservative lower bound is entered. The derived per-size ratios, 10/1.3 = 7.7 and 10/2.2 = 4.5, span the same range, and the second coder's 7.5 is the midpoint of the range, a coder construct.
